• Render is not the same as a DOM update: a component can re-render without changing the DOM.
• StrictMode renders twice in development to expose impure components.

interviewQA: What is the virtual DOM?
A lightweight tree of React elements describing the UI. React compares the new tree with the previous one (diffing) and updates only the real DOM nodes that changed.
Why must components be pure?

React may render a component several times (StrictMode, concurrent rendering) and expects the same output for the same inputs. Side effects during render cause bugs; put them in event handlers or useEffect.
Why should you not define a component inside another component?
Each render creates a new function, so React sees a different component type, unmounts the old one and mounts a new one, destroying its state and hurting performance.

topics.name: Class Components and the Component Lifecycle

beginner.content:
Class components (legacy, but still in many codebases)

• Before hooks, stateful components were classes extending React.Component, with this.props, this.state, this.setState() and a render() method.
• New code should use function components with hooks, but you must read class components in older projects. Error boundaries still require a class.
• setState merges the update into state and is asynchronous/batched: use setState(prev => ...) when the new state depends on the old.

intermediate.content:
Lifecycle phases and their hook equivalents

PhaseClass methodFunction component
Mounting (first render)constructor, render, componentDidMountuseEffect(() => {...}, [])
Updating (props/state change)render, componentDidUpdate(prevProps, prevState)useEffect(() => {...}, [dep])
UnmountingcomponentWillUnmountcleanup function returned from useEffect
ErrorgetDerivedStateFromError, componentDidCatchno hook; use an error boundary class
• Fetch data and subscribe in componentDidMount; clean up in componentWillUnmount; compare previous and current values in componentDidUpdate to avoid loops.

expert.content:
Why hooks replaced classes

• Logic in classes is split across lifecycle methods by time (mount, update, unmount); with hooks it is grouped by concern (one effect per subscription), and reusable through custom hooks.
• Classes need this binding and wrapper patterns (HOCs, render props) for reuse, which create deep trees.
• Migrating: convert class to function, this.state to useState, lifecycle methods to useEffect, instance fields to useRef. Keep boundary components as classes (or use react-error-boundary).
• Legacy lifecycle methods componentWillMount, componentWillReceiveProps, componentWillUpdate are deprecated (unsafe with concurrent rendering).

interviewQA: What are the lifecycle phases of a React component?

Mounting (created and inserted into the DOM), updating (re-rendered after props or state change) and unmounting (removed). Class components have methods for each; function components use useEffect and its cleanup.
Which hook replaces componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate and componentWillUnmount?
useEffect: an empty dependency array runs after mount, a populated array runs after relevant updates, and the returned cleanup function runs on unmount (and before re-running).
Why are class components discouraged for new code?
Hooks make logic reusable and grouped by concern, avoid this-binding problems and wrapper hell, and work better with concurrent rendering. Classes remain only for error boundaries.

topics.name: Props: Passing Data Down

beginner.content:
Props are the inputs of a component

• Props are passed like HTML attributes and received as one object, usually destructured in the parameter list.
• Props flow one way: parent to child, and are read-only. A child that needs to change something calls a function the parent passed down.
• You can pass any value: strings, numbers, booleans (disabled alone means true), objects, arrays, functions and even JSX. Non-string values need braces.

intermediate.content:
Defaults, rest props and the children prop

• Default values in destructuring: ({ size = 48 }). Collect leftovers with rest: ({ label, ...rest }) and forward them: <button {...rest}>.
• children is whatever you put between the tags: text, elements or functions. It makes wrapper components (Card, Modal, Layout) flexible.
• Do not copy a prop into state "to edit it later" unless you intend it as an initial value (name it initialValue): the copy will not follow later prop changes.

expert.content:
Prop pitfalls

• Mutating props (props.items.push(x)) breaks one-way data flow. Props are read-only.
• Inline objects/functions create a new reference every render, defeating React.memo. Stabilise with useMemo/useCallback only when profiling shows a need.
• Passing too many props is a smell: group related ones into an object, or use composition/Context.
• Validate props: with TypeScript (preferred) or PropTypes in JavaScript projects.

interviewQA: Can a child change its props?
No. Props are read-only. To change data the child calls a callback passed from the parent, which updates the parent's state and re-renders the child with new props.
What is the children prop?
The content placed between a component's opening and closing tags. It lets a component wrap arbitrary content, such as Card, Layout or Modal.
Why not copy props into state?
The state copy is initialised once and does not update when the prop changes, so the two drift apart. Derive values from props during render, or treat the prop explicitly as an initial value.

topics.name: Composition Patterns: Slots, Render Props and Compound Components

beginner.content:
Composition over inheritance

• React reuses UI by composing components, never by inheriting from them. Build general components that accept children or other elements as props, and specialise by wrapping.
• Slots: pass JSX through named props (header, footer) for layouts with several holes.

intermediate.content:
Render props and the container/presentational split

• A render prop is a function prop that returns JSX, letting the child component supply data while the parent decides how to display it. Hooks replaced most uses, but the pattern is still useful for lists and layout.
• Separate logic (fetching, state) from presentation (markup). Keep presentational components pure and easy to test; put logic in custom hooks or container components.

expert.content:
Compound components

• A compound component is a set of components that work together and share implicit state, like <select>/<option>: <Tabs>, <Tabs.List>, <Tabs.Panel>. The parent owns the state and shares it through Context, so users get a flexible, declarative API.
• Design rules: keep the public API small, let consumers control layout through composition, and document required nesting.

interviewQA: Composition vs inheritance in React?
React favours composition: build components from other components using props and children. Inheritance between components is not recommended; shared logic goes into composition or custom hooks.
What is a render prop?
A prop whose value is a function returning JSX, used so a component can share its internal data while the consumer controls what is rendered.
What is a compound component?
A group of related components (Tabs, Tab, Panel) that share state implicitly, usually via Context, giving a flexible declarative API similar to select/option.

topics.name: State with useState: Snapshots, Batching and Updater Functions

beginner.content:
State is a component's memory

• const [value, setValue] = useState(initial) returns the current value and a setter. Calling the setter schedules a re-render with the new value.
• A normal local variable is reset every render and changing it does not update the screen; state survives re-renders and triggers them.
• Each component instance has its own state: two <Counter /> elements count independently.

intermediate.content:
State is a snapshot; updates are batched

• Within one render, count has a fixed value (a snapshot). setCount(count + 1) three times adds only 1 because all three read the same snapshot.
• Use the updater function when the next value depends on the previous one: setCount(c => c + 1).
• React batches updates from one event into a single render. The state variable still holds the old value right after calling the setter in the same handler.
• Initial value from an expensive computation: pass a function (lazy initial state): useState(() => readFromStorage()).

expert.content:
Choosing and structuring state

• Do not store derived data: compute filtered, total or fullName during render from existing state instead of keeping another state variable in sync.
• Group related fields into one object ({x, y}) or use useReducer; avoid contradictory booleans (isLoading and isError both true): prefer one status string.
• Avoid duplicated and deeply nested state: store IDs and look objects up, or normalise.
• Keep state as low as possible; lift it to the nearest common parent only when needed.
• Setting the same value (by Object.is) skips the re-render.

interviewQA: Why does setCount(count + 1) three times only add one?
Inside one render count is a snapshot, so each call computes the same next value. Use setCount(c => c + 1) so each update receives the latest value.
What is derived state and why avoid storing it?
Values computable from props/state (totals, filtered lists). Storing them duplicates truth and can go out of sync; compute them during render instead.
What is lazy initial state?
Passing a function to useState(() => expensive()) so the initial value is computed only on the first render instead of on every render.

topics.name: Event Handling: Handlers, Synthetic Events and Arguments

beginner.content:
Reacting to the user

• Attach handlers with camelCase props: onClick, onChange, onSubmit, onKeyDown. Pass a function, do not call it: onClick={handle}, not onClick={handle()}.
• The handler receives a SyntheticEvent, a cross-browser wrapper with the same API as the native event (e.target, e.preventDefault(), e.stopPropagation()).
• Handlers are where side effects (setting state, calling APIs) belong.

intermediate.content:
Passing arguments and the classic mistakes

• To pass an argument, wrap the call in an arrow function: onClick={() => remove(item.id)}.
• onClick={remove(item.id)} runs remove during render, usually causing an infinite loop of re-renders.
• Event handlers can be passed as props (onSelect) so children report events to the parent. Name props onXxx and handlers handleXxx.
• In a form, a <button> without type="button" submits the form.

expert.content:
Propagation, delegation and async events

• Events bubble up the component tree: a click on a button also triggers its parents' onClick. Stop it with e.stopPropagation(); use onClickCapture for the capture phase.
• React attaches one listener at the root (event delegation), so you never add or remove listeners yourself.
• Since React 17 there is no event pooling: you can read e asynchronously. Still, read the values you need first (const value = e.target.value) before awaiting.
• For non-React DOM events (window resize, keydown on document) use useEffect with cleanup.

interviewQA: What is a SyntheticEvent?
React's cross-browser wrapper around the native event with the same interface (preventDefault, stopPropagation, target). Handlers receive it as their argument.
Why does onClick={handle()} cause an infinite loop?
It calls handle during rendering and passes its return value. If handle sets state, that triggers another render, which calls it again. Pass the function itself or wrap it in an arrow.
How do you handle window-level events in React?
Register them in useEffect with addEventListener and remove them in the cleanup function, so listeners do not leak or duplicate.

topics.name: Lifting State Up and useReducer

beginner.content:
Sharing state between components

• When two components need the same data, lift the state up to their closest common parent. The parent passes the value down as a prop and a setter (callback) down for changes.
• Data flows down, events flow up ("inverse data flow").

intermediate.content:
useReducer for complex transitions

• const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initial) puts all state transitions in one pure function (state, action) => newState. Use it when state has several fields that change together or when the next state depends on a named event.
• Reducers must be pure and must not mutate state; actions are plain objects with a type.
• Benefits: all update logic in one testable place, clearer than many useState calls, easy to pair with Context.

expert.content:
Choosing where state lives

• Decision guide: used by one component → local useState; shared by a few nearby components → lift up; needed across distant parts → Context or a store; comes from the server → TanStack Query/SWR, not useState.
• URL state (filters, page, tab) belongs in the URL (search params) so it is shareable and survives refresh.
• Form state can stay uncontrolled or in a form library.
• Avoid "prop drilling" through many layers by composition (pass elements/children) before reaching for Context.

interviewQA: What does lifting state up mean?
Moving state from a child to the nearest common ancestor so several children can read it (via props) and change it (via callbacks), keeping a single source of truth.
When would you choose useReducer over useState?
When state is an object/array with several related updates or when the next state depends on named actions; it centralises logic in a pure reducer and is easy to test.
What is prop drilling and how do you avoid it?
Passing props through many intermediate components that do not use them. Avoid with composition (children/slots), Context for truly global values, or a state library.

topics.name: Conditional Rendering Patterns

beginner.content:
Showing UI based on conditions

• JSX has no if statement, but you can use plain JavaScript: early return, ternary cond ? <A /> : <B /> and logical AND cond && <A />.
• Returning null renders nothing.
• Use early returns for loading/error/empty states to keep the main JSX flat.

intermediate.content:
Pitfalls with && and nested ternaries

• {count && <Badge />} renders the number 0 when count is 0 (0 is falsy but renderable). Use a boolean: count > 0 && ....
• Nested ternaries get unreadable fast: extract a small function or component, or use a lookup object.
• Conditionally rendering removes the element and its state; conditionally hiding with CSS keeps it mounted. Choose deliberately (e.g. keep a tab's form state by hiding).

expert.content:
Patterns for larger apps

• Feature flags / permissions: wrap checks in a small component (<Can permission="edit">) so rules live in one place.
• Suspense and error boundaries handle loading and failures declaratively around subtrees.
• Switch-like components (<Match>) and discriminated unions (TypeScript) make every state explicit and exhaustive.
• Never put conditional hook calls inside branches: conditions apply to JSX, not to hooks.

interviewQA: Why does {count && <X />} sometimes show a 0?
Because 0 is falsy, so the expression evaluates to 0, and React renders numbers. Use a boolean condition such as count > 0.
Conditional rendering vs hiding with CSS?
Not rendering unmounts the component and discards its state and effects; hiding with CSS keeps it mounted (state preserved) but still in the DOM.
Can you call a hook inside an if?
No. Hooks must run in the same order on every render, so they cannot be placed inside conditions, loops or nested functions.

topics.name: Rendering Lists and Keys

beginner.content:
Turning arrays into UI

• Use array.map() to return one element per item. Every element in the list needs a key prop: a stable, unique value among siblings, typically the database id.
• Keys are not props: the child cannot read props.key. Put the key on the outermost element returned by map.

intermediate.content:
Why keys matter

• React uses keys to match items between renders. With stable keys it can move, insert and remove DOM nodes and keep each row's state (input text, focus). With index keys on a list that reorders, state sticks to the wrong row.
• Never generate keys during render (Math.random()): every render looks like all items were replaced, remounting everything.
• Use the index only for static lists that never reorder, filter or insert.
• Use <Fragment key={id}> when a list item renders multiple siblings.

expert.content:
Derived lists: filter, sort, group, paginate

• Keep the source list and the controls (query, sort order, page) in state; compute the visible list during render. Memoise with useMemo only for big data.
• Always render an empty state, and show how many results matched.
• Sort a copy, never the state array. For large lists use virtualisation (react-window) and server-side pagination.
• Group with reduce or Object.groupBy before mapping.

interviewQA: Why does React need keys in lists?
To identify each item across renders so it can reorder, add and remove DOM nodes efficiently and keep item state attached to the right item.
Is using the array index as a key okay?
Only for static lists that never reorder, filter or insert. Otherwise item identity shifts and state/inputs end up on the wrong rows. Use a stable unique id.
How do you implement search, sort and pagination over a list?
Store the source data and control values (query, sort, page) in state, derive the visible list during render (filter, sorted copy, slice), and render an empty state when nothing matches.

topics.name: useEffect: Side Effects, Dependencies and Cleanup

beginner.content:
Synchronising with the outside world

• An effect runs after React has rendered and committed to the DOM. Use it for things outside React: network requests, subscriptions, timers, manual DOM work, document.title, third-party widgets.
• useEffect(setup, deps): with [] it runs once after mount; with [a, b] after mount and whenever a or b change; with no array after every render.
• Return a cleanup function; it runs before the effect re-runs and on unmount.

intermediate.content:
Dependency rules and common bugs

• Every reactive value used inside the effect (props, state, functions defined in the component) must be in the dependency array. The ESLint rule react-hooks/exhaustive-deps checks this. Do not silence it; restructure instead.
• Infinite loop: setting state inside an effect that depends on that state, or an object/array/function created in render listed as a dependency (a new reference each time).
• Stale closure: an effect with missing deps keeps the old values; use the functional setter (setN(n => n + 1)) or add the dependency.
• Race conditions: when an input changes quickly, an older request may finish last. Ignore stale responses with a flag or AbortController in cleanup.

expert.content:
You might not need an effect

• Do not use effects to transform data for rendering (compute it in render), to handle user events (use handlers), or to reset state when a prop changes (use a key).
• Use effects for synchronisation: connect to a chat server, subscribe to a store, start an animation. Prefer useSyncExternalStore for external stores and a data library (TanStack Query) for server data.
• In development StrictMode runs setup, cleanup, setup on mount to check that your cleanup is correct. This is intentional.
• useLayoutEffect runs before paint (measure the DOM, avoid flicker); useInsertionEffect is for CSS-in-JS libraries.

interviewQA: What does the dependency array do?
It lists the reactive values the effect reads. React re-runs the effect after a render where any of them changed ([] = only after mount, omitted = after every render).
Why does my effect run twice in development?
StrictMode intentionally mounts, unmounts and remounts components to reveal missing cleanup. It does not happen in production builds.
When should you NOT use useEffect?
For computing values from props/state (derive in render), responding to user events (use handlers) and resetting state on prop change (use key). Effects are for synchronising with external systems.

topics.name: useRef, useMemo, useCallback and Friends

beginner.content:
useRef: values that do not trigger renders

• const ref = useRef(initial) gives a stable object { current } that persists across renders. Changing ref.current does not re-render.
• Two uses: (1) reach a DOM node (<input ref={ref} /> then ref.current.focus()), (2) hold mutable values that are not part of the UI (timer ids, previous value, latest callback).
• Never read or write ref.current during render (except to initialise).

intermediate.content:
useMemo and useCallback: caching

• useMemo(() => compute(a, b), [a, b]) caches a value until a dependency changes. useCallback(fn, deps) caches a function (same as useMemo(() => fn, deps)).
• Use them when (1) a calculation is genuinely expensive, or (2) a value/function is passed to a React.memo child or is a dependency of another hook and its identity matters.
• They are optimisations, not guarantees: your code must work without them. Measure before adding. Overuse adds complexity and memory cost for no gain.

expert.content:
More built-in hooks

• useId: unique, SSR-safe ids for label/input pairs and ARIA attributes.
• useTransition / useDeferredValue: keep typing responsive while a heavy update renders in the background.
• useSyncExternalStore: subscribe to external stores safely (used by state libraries).
• useImperativeHandle with forwardRef (or a ref prop in React 19): expose a small imperative API (focus(), reset()) from a component.
• use (React 19) reads a promise or context during render, integrating with Suspense.

interviewQA: useRef vs useState?

Both persist across renders, but changing state re-renders the component while changing ref.current does not. Use state for data shown in the UI and refs for DOM nodes and non-visual values like timer ids.
useMemo vs useCallback?
useMemo caches a computed value, useCallback caches a function. Both rely on the dependency array and are performance optimisations, not semantic guarantees.
When is React.memo useful?
When a component re-renders often with the same props and its render is costly. It compares props shallowly, so object/function props must keep stable identity (useMemo/useCallback) for it to help.

topics.name: Custom Hooks and the Rules of Hooks

beginner.content:
Rules of Hooks

• Call hooks only at the top level of a component or a custom hook: not inside loops, conditions, nested functions or after an early return.
• Call hooks only from React function components or custom hooks, never from regular functions or classes.
• React identifies each hook by its call order; the rules guarantee the order is identical on every render. Install eslint-plugin-react-hooks to enforce them.

intermediate.content:
Writing custom hooks

• A custom hook is a function whose name starts with use and that calls other hooks. It shares logic, not state: each component that calls it gets its own state.
• Typical candidates: data fetching (useFetch), form handling (useForm), useLocalStorage, useDebounce, useOnlineStatus, useMediaQuery, useClickOutside.
• Return what the consumer needs: a value, a tuple [value, setValue] or an object. Keep the API small.

expert.content:
Design guidelines and a fetch hook

• Name hooks after what they do (useUser, not useData). Do not create "lifecycle" hooks like useMount: they hide dependencies.
• Hooks compose: a hook can use other hooks. Test them with renderHook from React Testing Library.
• Mind the closure: hooks that accept a callback should keep the latest callback in a ref to avoid stale values, without forcing the effect to re-subscribe.
• For server data prefer a mature library (TanStack Query); a handwritten useFetch is a good learning tool.

interviewQA: What are the rules of hooks and why do they exist?
Call hooks only at the top level of function components/custom hooks and never conditionally. React tracks hooks by call order, so the order must be identical on every render.
Do custom hooks share state between components?
No. They share logic only; every component calling the hook gets its own independent state and effects.
How do you test a custom hook?
With renderHook from @testing-library/react: render the hook, call its returned functions inside act(), and assert on result.current.

topics.name: Controlled and Uncontrolled Forms

beginner.content:
Controlled components

• A controlled input gets its value from state and updates it in onChange. React is the single source of truth, so you can validate, format or reject input on every keystroke.
• Checkboxes use checked; <select> and <textarea> use value.
• One state object plus one handler keyed by the input name scales to many fields.

intermediate.content:
Uncontrolled forms and FormData

• An uncontrolled input keeps its own DOM state; you read it on submit via a ref or FormData. Fewer re-renders and less code for simple forms; defaultValue sets the initial value.
• File inputs (type="file") are always uncontrolled.
• Do not switch an input between controlled and uncontrolled (value from undefined to a string): initialise state with "".
• React 19 form Actions: <form action={fn}> calls fn(formData), with useActionState and useFormStatus for pending state and results.

expert.content:
Submit states and good UX

• Track status (idle | submitting | success | error), disable the submit button while submitting to prevent double posts, and show server errors next to the form.
• Reset the form after success; keep entered values after failure.
• Use proper input types and attributes (type="email", autoComplete, inputMode) so mobile keyboards and password managers work.
• Associate every input with a <label> (htmlFor/id or wrap) for accessibility.

interviewQA: Controlled vs uncontrolled inputs?

Controlled inputs take value from React state and update it onChange. Uncontrolled inputs keep their value in the DOM and you read it with a ref or FormData. Controlled gives per-keystroke control; uncontrolled is simpler and lighter.
Why does React warn about switching from uncontrolled to controlled?
The input started with value undefined (uncontrolled) and later got a defined value. Initialise state with an empty string so the input is controlled from the first render.
How do you prevent double submission?
Track a submitting status, disable the submit button (and ignore re-entry) while the request is pending, and re-enable it after success or failure.

topics.name: Form Validation: Manual, React Hook Form and Zod

beginner.content:
Validating by hand

• Validate on submit at minimum; improve UX by validating a field on blur and re-validating on change once it has been touched.
• Keep an errors object keyed by field name and render the message next to the input with aria-invalid and aria-describedby.
• Put validation rules in a pure function so they can be unit-tested and reused on the server.

intermediate.content:
React Hook Form with Zod

• React Hook Form uses uncontrolled inputs internally, so large forms stay fast. It manages registration, touched/dirty state, errors and submit status.
• Zod defines a schema once; z.infer gives the TypeScript type; zodResolver connects it to the form. The same schema can validate the API request on a Node server.

expert.content:
Server-side validation, dynamic fields and accessibility

• Client validation is for convenience; the server must validate again. Map server error responses (HTTP 400/422 with field messages) back onto fields with setError("email", { message }).
• Dynamic lists of fields: useFieldArray (add/remove rows). Multi-step wizards: keep one form state, validate per step.
• Accessibility: label every field, announce errors with role="alert" or an aria-live region, move focus to the first invalid field on submit, do not rely on colour alone.
• Debounce asynchronous checks (is this username taken?) and show a pending state.

interviewQA: Why use React Hook Form instead of useState for forms?
It registers inputs as uncontrolled, minimising re-renders, and provides validation, error and submission state out of the box with little code, which scales to large forms.
Is client-side validation enough?
No. It can be bypassed. Always validate on the server too, and show server-side errors on the corresponding fields.
How do you make form errors accessible?
Associate messages with fields using aria-describedby/aria-invalid, announce them with role="alert" or aria-live, and move focus to the first invalid input after a failed submit.

topics.name: React Router: Routes, Links and Parameters

beginner.content:
Client-side routing

• A single-page app has one HTML page. React Router maps URLs to components and updates the address bar without a page reload (History API).
• Install: npm install react-router-dom. Wrap the app in a router and declare <Route path element> entries.
• Use <Link to>/<NavLink> (never a plain <a href> for internal links, which reloads the page). NavLink adds an active class.

intermediate.content:
URL parameters, query strings and navigation

• Path params: path="/courses/:courseId" and useParams() (always strings: convert numbers).
• Query string: useSearchParams() for filters, sort and page. Putting UI state in the URL makes it shareable and survives refresh.
• Programmatic navigation: useNavigate() (navigate("/courses"), navigate(-1)); pass state with navigate(to, { state }) and read it with useLocation().
• Redirect declaratively with <Navigate to="/login" replace />.

expert.content:
How it works and server setup

• BrowserRouter uses clean URLs and needs the server to return index.html for unknown paths; otherwise a refresh on /courses/5 gives a 404. (Spring Boot: forward non-file paths to index.html; nginx: try_files $uri /index.html.) HashRouter (/#/courses) avoids this but is uglier.
• Route ranking: React Router picks the most specific match, so order does not matter. * catches everything else (404 page).
• Scroll position and focus management on navigation need attention: restore scroll with <ScrollRestoration /> (data routers) and move focus to the page heading for accessibility.

interviewQA: Why use Link instead of an anchor tag?
A plain <a href> triggers a full page load. Link intercepts the click and uses the History API to change the URL and render the new route without reloading, keeping app state.
Why does refreshing /courses/5 give a 404 in production?
The server has no such file. For client-side routing the server must return index.html for all non-API, non-file paths so React Router can handle the route.
useParams vs useSearchParams?
useParams reads dynamic segments of the path (/courses/:id). useSearchParams reads and writes the query string (?tab=reviews&page=2).

topics.name: Nested Routes, Layouts and Protected Routes

beginner.content:
Layout routes and Outlet

• Nest routes to share UI. A layout route renders common chrome (header, sidebar) and an <Outlet /> where the matching child route appears.
• Index routes (index) render at the parent's path. Child paths are relative to the parent.

intermediate.content:
Protecting routes

• A protected route redirects unauthenticated users to login and remembers where they wanted to go. Implement it as a layout route that renders <Outlet /> or <Navigate>.
• Wait for the auth check to finish (loading state) before redirecting, or users with a valid session get bounced.
• Client-side checks are not security: the API must enforce authorisation on the server.

expert.content:
Data routers: loaders, actions and lazy routes

• createBrowserRouter + RouterProvider enable loaders (fetch data before rendering a route), actions (handle form submissions) and route-level errorElement. This removes many useEffect fetches and loading flashes.
• Lazy routes (lazy: () => import("./Reports")) split code per page.
• useNavigation().state tells you when a navigation or submission is pending (show a top progress bar).

interviewQA: What is an Outlet?
A placeholder in a parent (layout) route component where the matching child route's element is rendered, enabling shared layouts.
How do you protect a route in React Router?

Create a layout route that checks authentication (and roles) and renders <Outlet /> if allowed, otherwise <Navigate to="/login" />. Remember the API must enforce authorisation, since client checks can be bypassed.
What are loaders?
Functions on data-router routes that fetch data before the route renders. Components read it with useLoaderData, avoiding fetch-in-effect waterfalls and loading flashes.

topics.name: Fetching Data: Loading, Error and Empty States

beginner.content:
The three faces of every request

• Every data-driven screen has at least four states: loading, error, empty and success. Handle all of them.
• Basic pattern: store data, error and status in state, fetch inside useEffect and abort on cleanup.
• Check response.ok; fetch does not reject on HTTP errors.

intermediate.content:
An API client module

• Centralise HTTP in one module: base URL from import.meta.env, JSON headers, auth header, error normalisation and a typed result. Components then call api.get("/users").
• Axios is a popular alternative (interceptors, automatic JSON, timeouts), but fetch is enough with a small wrapper.
• Normalise errors into one shape (status, message, fieldErrors) so the UI can treat them uniformly.

expert.content:
Race conditions, retries and CORS

• When parameters change quickly (search), an older response can arrive after a newer one: abort the previous request in cleanup.
• Retry only idempotent requests (GET) and only for network/5xx errors, with exponential backoff.
• In development a request from localhost:5173 to localhost:3001 is cross-origin: use a Vite proxy or enable CORS on the server (Spring Boot CorsConfigurationSource) with explicit allowed origins.
• Do not fire a request on every keystroke: debounce.

interviewQA: What states must a data-fetching component handle?
Loading, error, empty and success. Showing only the success case leaves users with blank screens or crashes on failure.
How do you avoid a stale response overwriting a newer one?
Abort the previous request in the effect cleanup (AbortController) or ignore its result with a cancelled flag, so only the latest request updates state.
Why create an API client module?
It keeps base URL, headers, auth, error handling and JSON parsing in one place, so components stay small and behaviour is consistent and easy to change.

topics.name: TanStack Query: Caching, Mutations and Optimistic Updates

beginner.content:
Server state is not client state

• Data from an API is a cache of remote state that can become stale, be shared by many components and needs refetching. Managing it with useState + useEffect means rewriting caching, de-duplication, retries and refetch logic.
• TanStack Query (React Query) provides all of that: useQuery for reads, useMutation for writes, a QueryClient cache keyed by query keys.

intermediate.content:
Query keys and mutations

• The query key identifies the cache entry: include every variable the request depends on (["users", { page, search }]). When a key changes, a new request is made (and the old data can be shown meanwhile with placeholderData).
• useMutation performs create/update/delete. After success, invalidate related queries so they refetch: queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["users"] }).
• staleTime controls how long data counts as fresh; gcTime how long unused data stays cached.

expert.content:
Optimistic updates, infinite lists and prefetching

• Optimistic update: apply the change to the cache immediately (onMutate), roll back on error (onError) and refetch to reconcile (onSettled). The UI feels instant.
• useInfiniteQuery implements "load more"/infinite scroll with cursors or pages.
• prefetchQuery on hover or in a router loader warms the cache so navigation feels immediate.
• Put auth handling in the API client (refresh token on 401), not in each query.

interviewQA: Why use TanStack Query instead of useEffect + useState?
It handles caching, request de-duplication, background refetching, retries, pagination, optimistic updates and loading/error states, which are tedious and error-prone to implement by hand.
What is a query key?
An array identifying a cache entry. It must include every input of the request; changing it triggers a new fetch and gives each variation its own cached data.
How does an optimistic update work?
Update the cache immediately in onMutate (keeping a snapshot), roll back in onError if the request fails, and invalidate/refetch in onSettled so the UI matches the server.

topics.name: Authentication and Spring Boot Integration

beginner.content:
Talking to a Spring Boot API

• A typical stack: React (Vite, port 5173) + Spring Boot REST API (port 8080/3001). In development, proxy /api to the server; in production serve the built React files from the same origin (Spring Boot static resources or nginx) so no CORS is needed.
• Match the contract: JSON field names, status codes (201 + Location on create, 204 on delete, 400/422 for validation), and pagination shape (page, size, totalElements).
• Generate TypeScript types from the OpenAPI spec (springdoc) to keep both sides in sync.

intermediate.content:
Authentication patterns

• Session cookie (recommended for browser apps): the server sets an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite cookie after login. JavaScript cannot read it, so XSS cannot steal it. Call APIs with credentials: "include" and protect against CSRF (SameSite, CSRF token).
• JWT in the Authorization header: keep the short-lived access token in memory, the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie. Avoid localStorage for tokens.
• Expose the current user through an AuthContext (user, login, logout, loading) loaded from /api/me at start-up.

expert.content:
Handling 401, 403 and refresh tokens centrally

• 401 = not authenticated (log in again or refresh); 403 = authenticated but not allowed (show a "no access" page).
• Handle these once in the API client: on 401 try a single refresh, retry the original request, else clear the user and redirect to login. Serialise concurrent refreshes so only one runs.
• Show friendly messages for 429 (rate limited) and offline errors; keep technical details in logs.

interviewQA: Where should a React app store authentication tokens?

Prefer HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies set by the server. If you use JWTs, keep the short-lived access token in memory and the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie; avoid localStorage because XSS can read it.
401 Unauthorized means the request lacks valid authentication (log in or refresh); 403 Forbidden means the user is authenticated but not permitted. The UI reacts differently to each.
How do you avoid CORS problems in development and production?

Proxy /api through the Vite dev server in development and serve the built front end from the same origin as the API in production. If cross-origin is required, configure CORS on the server with explicit origins.

topics.name: Axios: Instances, Interceptors and Fetch vs Axios

beginner.content:
What Axios adds to fetch

• Axios is a promise-based HTTP client (npm i axios). Compared with fetch it parses JSON automatically, rejects on HTTP error statuses (4xx/5xx), supports timeouts, request cancellation, upload progress, and interceptors.
• The result is in response.data. Errors expose error.response.status and error.response.data (server answered with an error) or error.request (no response: network problem).
• Methods: axios.get(url, config), axios.post(url, body, config), put, patch, delete.

intermediate.content:
An Axios instance with interceptors

• Create one configured instance (axios.create) with the base URL, timeout and credentials, and use it everywhere.
• Request interceptor: attach the auth header or a request id. Response interceptor: handle 401 (refresh token and retry once), normalise errors, show global toasts.
• Interceptors keep cross-cutting concerns out of components.

expert.content:
Cancellation, uploads and choosing between fetch and Axios

• Cancel with AbortController: axios.get(url, { signal }); handle axios.isCancel(err) / err.code === "ERR_CANCELED". Use it in useEffect cleanup.
• Upload progress: onUploadProgress with FormData; download progress: onDownloadProgress.
• fetch: built in, no dependency, works in service workers and edge runtimes, streaming. Axios: less boilerplate, interceptors, automatic error rejection, progress events. Both work well with TanStack Query: only the queryFn changes.
• Do not mix styles in one project: pick one and wrap it in an API module.

interviewQA: What does Axios do that fetch does not?
Automatic JSON parsing, rejection on 4xx/5xx statuses, built-in timeouts, request/response interceptors, upload/download progress and a consistent error object.
What is an Axios interceptor?
A function that runs before every request or after every response, used for cross-cutting work such as adding the Authorization header, refreshing tokens on 401, logging and normalising errors.
How do you cancel an Axios request?
Pass an AbortController signal in the config and call abort() (for example in the useEffect cleanup); the promise rejects with a cancellation error that axios.isCancel recognises.

topics.name: CRUD Operations: React + Spring Boot Project

beginner.content:
CRUD maps to HTTP

• Create = POST /api/courses (201 Created), Read = GET /api/courses and GET /api/courses/{id} (200), Update = PUT (replace) or PATCH (partial), Delete = DELETE /api/courses/{id} (204 No Content).
• The Spring Boot side: a @RestController, a service layer, a JPA repository and DTOs with Bean Validation (@NotBlank, @Size).
• The React side: a list page, a create/edit form and a delete action, all sharing one API module.

intermediate.content:
The React screens with TanStack Query

• List: useQuery(["courses", {q, page}]). Create/Update: useMutation, then invalidate ["courses"] so the list refetches. Delete: confirm, mutate, invalidate.
• Reuse one form component for create and edit: pass initialValues and onSubmit.
• Map server validation errors (HTTP 400/422) onto the fields.

expert.content:
Production concerns for CRUD

• Validation on both sides: Bean Validation on the server is the truth; the React form gives fast feedback. Return a consistent error body ({ status, message, errors: { field: "message" } }) from a @ControllerAdvice.
• Pagination, sorting and filtering on the server; never load unbounded lists.
• Concurrency: add a version field (JPA @Version) so two users editing the same record get a 409 Conflict instead of silently overwriting each other.
• Authorization: enforce ownership/roles in the service layer; the UI hiding a Delete button is cosmetic.
• Idempotency: PUT and DELETE are safe to retry; POST is not (use an idempotency key for payments).
• Soft delete (a deleted flag) when data must be recoverable or audited.

interviewQA: Which HTTP methods and status codes does a REST CRUD API use?
POST (201 Created with Location) to create, GET (200) to read, PUT/PATCH (200) to update, DELETE (204 No Content) to remove; 400/422 for validation errors, 404 when missing, 409 for conflicts.
How do you keep the list fresh after creating or deleting a record?
With TanStack Query, call queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["courses"] }) in the mutation's onSuccess so the list refetches from the server.
How do you handle two users editing the same record?
Use optimistic locking: a version field (JPA @Version) that the client sends back. If it changed, the server returns 409 Conflict and the UI asks the user to reload and retry.

subTopics.name: Phase 10 · TypeScript with React (Essential for your chosen stack)

topics.name: TypeScript Fundamentals: Types, Interfaces and Type Aliases

beginner.content:
JavaScript with a type checker

• TypeScript adds static types to JavaScript. The compiler finds mistakes (wrong argument, missing property, possible undefined) before the code runs, then erases the types, leaving plain JavaScript.
• Basic types: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, arrays (number[] or Array<number>), tuples [string, number], unknown (safe "anything"), any (turns checking off: avoid), void, never.
• Annotate function parameters and return types; let TypeScript infer local variables.

intermediate.content:
Interfaces, type aliases, unions and narrowing

• interface and type both describe object shapes. Optional properties use ?; immutable ones readonly. interface can be extended (extends) and merged; type can also name unions, tuples and computed types.
• A union string | number allows several types; literal types ("GET" | "POST") restrict to exact values; an intersection A & B combines types.
• Narrowing: typeof, instanceof, in and equality checks refine a union inside a branch.

expert.content:
Strict mode, discriminated unions and setup

• Turn on "strict": true in tsconfig.json: it enables strictNullChecks (no accidental undefined), noImplicitAny and more. It is the most valuable setting.
• Discriminated unions (a shared literal field such as kind or status) let switch narrow each case and give exhaustive checking with never.
• Types are erased at runtime: external data (API, localStorage) is not checked. Validate with Zod. Avoid as assertions and the non-null ! unless you truly know better than the compiler.
• Start a project: npm create vite@latest app -- --template react-ts; check types with npx tsc --noEmit.

interviewQA: interface vs type alias?
Both describe shapes. An interface can be extended and merged and suits object contracts; a type alias can also express unions, intersections, tuples and mapped/conditional types.
What does strictNullChecks do?
It stops null and undefined from being assigned to other types, forcing you to handle missing values explicitly and preventing the most common runtime "cannot read property of undefined" errors.
What is the difference between any and unknown?
any disables checking for that value. unknown accepts any value but must be narrowed (typeof, instanceof, schema validation) before use, so it remains type-safe.

topics.name: Typing Props, State and Events

beginner.content:
Typing components

• Create a project with the TypeScript template: npm create vite@latest app -- --template react-ts. Files are .tsx (JSX) and .ts.
• Type props with an interface or type; function components are just functions, so no React.FC is needed (it is optional and not recommended).
• Optional props use ?; children use React.ReactNode; callbacks are typed function signatures.

intermediate.content:
Typing state and events

• useState infers from the initial value; when the initial value is null/empty, give the type: useState<User | null>(null), useState<string[]>([]).
• Event handler types: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>, React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>, React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>, React.KeyboardEvent. Inline handlers are inferred automatically.
• useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null) for DOM refs; useRef<number>(0) for mutable values.

expert.content:
Props that mirror HTML elements

• Extend native element props instead of re-declaring them: React.ComponentProps<"button"> or React.ButtonHTMLAttributes<HTMLButtonElement>. Consumers then get disabled, aria-*, onClick and type for free.
• Discriminated unions make impossible prop combinations a compile error (e.g. a link needs href, a button needs onClick).
• Use as const and satisfies to keep literal types in configuration objects.

interviewQA: Should you use React.FC?
It is optional and generally not recommended: plain functions with typed props are simpler, infer the return type and avoid implicit children in older typings.
How do you type useState that starts as null?
Provide the union explicitly: useState<User | null>(null). Without it TypeScript infers null only and rejects later assignments.
How do you type a change handler?
React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> for inputs (React.ChangeEvent<HTMLSelectElement> for selects); for inline arrow handlers the type is inferred from the element.

topics.name: Typing Hooks, Context and Generic Components

beginner.content:
Custom hooks and context

• Return tuples with as const (or an explicit return type) so positions keep distinct types: return [value, setValue] as const.
• Context: create it with a default of null and a custom hook that throws if used outside the provider; this removes the need to null-check everywhere.
• useReducer infers from the reducer: type State and a discriminated union Action.

intermediate.content:
Generic components and hooks

• A generic component keeps types flowing from data to render callbacks: function List<T>(props: { items: T[]; render: (item: T) => ReactNode }).
• A generic hook like useLocalStorage<T> or useFetch<T> returns T typed data.
• Constrain generics with extends (T extends { id: number }) when the component needs certain fields.

expert.content:
Typing data from the network

• Compile-time types are not checked at runtime. A server response typed as User may still be wrong. Validate at the boundary with Zod and infer the type from the schema, so type and validator cannot drift.
• Model async state as a discriminated union ({status: "loading"} | {status: "error", error} | {status: "success", data}) so data is only accessible when it exists.
• Share types with the back end by generating them from the OpenAPI spec (Spring Boot + springdoc + openapi-typescript).
• Enable strict and noUncheckedIndexedAccess; avoid any and unnecessary as casts.

interviewQA: Why is a TypeScript type not enough for API data?
Types are erased at runtime and do not verify what the server returns. Validate responses with a schema library (Zod) and derive the type from it.
How do you type a Context safely?
createContext<Value | null>(null) plus a useX hook that throws when the value is null, so consumers always receive a non-null typed value.
What is a discriminated union and why use it for async state?
A union of object types sharing a literal field (status). TypeScript narrows on it, so data is available only in the success branch, preventing access to missing data.

topics.name: Context API: Patterns and Pitfalls

beginner.content:
Sharing data without prop drilling

• Context lets a value be read by any component below a Provider, without passing props through every level. Good for values many components need and that change rarely: theme, current user, language, feature flags.
• Three steps: createContext(default), wrap a subtree in <Ctx.Provider value={...}>, read with useContext(Ctx).
• Wrap it in a custom hook (useTheme()) and a provider component (ThemeProvider) to keep the API tidy.

intermediate.content:
The re-render pitfall and how to avoid it

• Every consumer re-renders whenever the Provider's value changes by reference. An inline object value={{ user, login }} is a new object on every Provider render, so all consumers re-render even if nothing changed.
• Fixes: useMemo the value; split contexts (state context vs actions/dispatch context, or one context per concern); keep frequently changing state out of Context (use a store).
• Context is not a state manager: it only transports a value. Pair it with useState/useReducer.

expert.content:
When Context is the wrong tool

• High-frequency updates (mouse position, form keystrokes, animation) re-render every consumer: use local state, a store with selectors (Zustand, Redux) or refs.
• Server data belongs in TanStack Query, not Context.
• Context defaults only apply when there is no Provider above; use null plus a throwing hook to detect missing providers.
• Multiple providers nest ("provider hell"): compose them into one AppProviders component.
• Since React 19 you can render <ThemeContext value={...}> directly and read context with use(Ctx), even conditionally.

interviewQA: What is Context for?
Passing values (theme, user, locale) to many components in a subtree without threading props through every level. It transports a value; state still lives in useState/useReducer.
Why do all consumers re-render when a Provider value changes?
Context compares the value by reference. A new object each render counts as a change, so every consumer re-renders. Memoise the value and split contexts to limit this.
When would you choose Redux/Zustand over Context?
For large, frequently updated shared state, when you need selectors (re-render only what changed), middleware, dev tools and a predictable update flow.

topics.name: Redux Toolkit: Slices, Store and Async Thunks

beginner.content:
Why a store?

• Redux keeps global state in one store, changed only by dispatching actions processed by reducers. It gives predictable updates, great dev tools (time travel) and a clear data flow for large apps.
• Redux Toolkit (RTK) is the official, modern way: less boilerplate, Immer built in (write "mutating" code), good defaults. Install: npm i @reduxjs/toolkit react-redux.
• Three pieces: configureStore, createSlice, Provider + hooks useSelector/useDispatch.

intermediate.content:
Using the store in components

• useSelector(state => state.cart.items) subscribes the component to that slice of state and re-renders only when the selected value changes. Select the smallest value you need.
• useDispatch() returns dispatch; call dispatch(added(product)).
• Derived values: write selector functions (and memoise with createSelector) rather than storing totals in state.
• Keep state serialisable (no Dates, functions, class instances).

expert.content:
Async logic: thunks and RTK Query

• createAsyncThunk wraps an async function and dispatches pending/fulfilled/rejected actions you handle in extraReducers.
• RTK Query (createApi) is built-in data fetching and caching, like TanStack Query: generated hooks, cache invalidation by tags, optimistic updates.
• Decision guide: server data → RTK Query or TanStack Query; shared client state → slices; local UI state → useState. Do not put everything in Redux.

interviewQA: What does Redux Toolkit add over plain Redux?

Less boilerplate and safer defaults: configureStore with dev tools and middleware, createSlice (actions and reducers together), Immer for simple immutable updates, createAsyncThunk and RTK Query for async work.
Why is mutating state inside createSlice reducers allowed?
Reducers receive an Immer draft. Immer records the changes and produces a new immutable state, so the code looks mutating but never mutates the real state.
useSelector pitfalls?
Selecting a new object/array on every call (e.g. state.items.filter(...)) makes the component re-render every time. Select primitives or memoise derived data with createSelector.

topics.name: Zustand, Local Storage and Session Storage

beginner.content:
Zustand: a small store

• Zustand is a minimal store with no providers and no boilerplate: create((set) => ({...})) returns a hook. Components subscribe with a selector and re-render only when the selected value changes.
• Great for mid-size apps where Redux feels heavy and Context re-renders too much.

intermediate.content:
Local Storage and Session Storage

• localStorage persists until cleared (shared across tabs of the origin); sessionStorage lasts for one tab session. Both store strings (about 5 MB) and are synchronous: setItem, getItem, removeItem.
• Wrap access in try/catch (private mode, quota) and JSON.parse safely. Initialise state lazily: useState(() => read()).
• Never store secrets (tokens, passwords): any XSS can read them. Use it for preferences, drafts and non-sensitive cache.
• Sync across tabs with the storage event.

expert.content:
Persisting stores and choosing a strategy

• Zustand and Redux have persistence helpers: persist middleware (Zustand) and redux-persist. Persist only the slices you need and add a version with a migration so old saved data does not crash a new release.
• For larger offline data use IndexedDB (idb, Dexie); for URL-shareable state use search params.
• Decision guide: local UI state → useState; shared client state → Context/Zustand/Redux; server state → TanStack Query/RTK Query; URL state → router; persistent preferences → storage via a store.

interviewQA: localStorage vs sessionStorage?
localStorage persists across browser sessions and is shared between tabs of the same origin; sessionStorage is per tab and cleared when the tab closes. Both store strings only.
Why not store a JWT in localStorage?
Any script on the page (including injected via XSS) can read localStorage. Prefer HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies or keep short-lived access tokens in memory.
How do you choose between Context, Zustand and Redux?

Context for rarely changing values; Zustand for simple shared state with selectors; Redux Toolkit for large apps needing strict structure, middleware and dev tools. Server data goes to a data-fetching library.

topics.name: Component Re-rendering and React.memo

beginner.content:
When does a component re-render?

• A component re-renders when its state changes, when its parent re-renders (even if its props are identical), or when a context it reads changes.
• Re-rendering means calling the function again to compute JSX; React then diffs and updates only changed DOM. Most re-renders are cheap and fine.
• Find real problems first: React DevTools Profiler ("Highlight updates", flamegraph) and the browser Performance tab. Optimise what is measurably slow.

intermediate.content:
React.memo and stable props

• React.memo(Component) skips re-rendering when the props are shallowly equal to last time.
• It only helps if props are stable: object, array and function props created inline are new each render and defeat memo. Stabilise with useMemo/useCallback, or move constants outside the component.
• Memoise components that are expensive to render, rendered many times (list rows) or deep in the tree. Do not wrap everything: comparing props has a cost.
• A custom comparison function is the second argument, but is rarely needed.

expert.content:
Structural fixes before memoising

• Move state down: put state in the smallest component that needs it so siblings are unaffected.
• Lift content up (children as props): a component that receives children does not re-render those children when its own state changes, because the elements were created by the parent.
• Split context and use selectors in stores.
• React Compiler (React 19+) can memoise automatically at build time; write straightforward, pure code and let it help.

interviewQA: What triggers a re-render in React?
A state change in the component, a re-render of its parent, or a change in a context value it consumes. Props changing is a consequence of the parent re-rendering.
When does React.memo not help?
When props change every render (inline objects/functions, new arrays). Then the shallow comparison always fails and the comparison cost is wasted. Stabilise props or fix the component structure.
How do you find performance problems in React?
Use the React DevTools Profiler to see which components render and why, and the browser Performance tab to see long tasks; measure before and after optimising.

topics.name: Lazy Loading, Suspense and Code Splitting

beginner.content:
Ship less JavaScript up front

• A big bundle delays the first screen. Code splitting breaks the app into chunks that load on demand. The bundler (Vite/Rollup, webpack) creates a chunk for every dynamic import().
• React.lazy(() => import("./Reports")) declares a lazily loaded component; wrap it in <Suspense fallback> to show a placeholder while the chunk downloads.
• Split by route first (biggest win), then by heavy widgets (charts, editors, maps).

intermediate.content:
Suspense boundaries, prefetching and error handling

• Place Suspense boundaries around the parts that load independently so one slow chunk does not blank the whole page; nest them for progressive reveal.
• Prefetch likely next chunks: call the import on hover/focus (onMouseEnter) or when idle, so navigation feels instant.
• Pair with an error boundary: a failed chunk download (offline, new deploy) throws, and you should offer a retry or reload.
• Lazy components must be default exports (or re-export them as default).

expert.content:
Analysing and shrinking the bundle

• Measure with a visualiser (rollup-plugin-visualizer, source-map-explorer) to see what is big. Typical culprits: moment.js (use date-fns/Day.js), whole lodash (import functions), icon libraries (import individual icons), duplicate versions of a library.
• Tree shaking removes unused exports from ES modules; import named exports, avoid side-effect-heavy barrels.
• Configure manualChunks to separate vendor libraries that rarely change, so browsers cache them across deploys.
• Compress (Brotli/gzip) and cache hashed assets for a year with Cache-Control: immutable.

interviewQA: What is code splitting?
Dividing the bundle into chunks loaded on demand, usually via dynamic import(), so users download only the code needed for the current page.
What does Suspense do with React.lazy?
While the lazy component's chunk is loading, Suspense renders the fallback UI; when the chunk arrives it renders the component.
How do you reduce bundle size?
Split by route, import only what you use (tree shaking, per-function imports), replace heavy libraries, analyse the bundle with a visualiser, compress assets and cache hashed files long-term.

topics.name: Performance Practices: Lists, Transitions, Images and Web Vitals

beginner.content:
Big lists and expensive renders

• Rendering thousands of rows is slow regardless of memoisation. Virtualise: render only the visible rows (react-window, @tanstack/react-virtual). Paginate on the server when possible.
• Use stable keys, avoid creating components in render, and keep render functions cheap (move heavy computation into useMemo or a Web Worker).
• Avoid anonymous function props to memoised children and avoid copying large arrays unnecessarily.

intermediate.content:
Keeping the UI responsive: transitions and debouncing

• useTransition marks a state update as non-urgent: React keeps the UI responsive (typing, clicking) and renders the heavy update in the background, with isPending for feedback.
• useDeferredValue(value) gives a lagging copy of a value for expensive subtrees.
• Debounce network calls and expensive filters; throttle scroll/resize handlers; use requestAnimationFrame for visual updates.

expert.content:
Images, fonts, network and Core Web Vitals

• Core Web Vitals: LCP (loading, aim under 2.5 s), INP (interaction latency, under 200 ms), CLS (layout shift, under 0.1). Measure with Lighthouse, PageSpeed Insights and the web-vitals library.
• Images: modern formats (AVIF/WebP), correct sizes and width/height (prevents layout shift), loading="lazy" below the fold, fetchpriority="high" for the hero image.
• Fonts: font-display: swap, self-host, preload the critical font.
• Network: HTTP caching, CDN, compression, avoid request waterfalls (fetch in parallel, prefetch), and use a service worker for repeat visits.

interviewQA: What is list virtualisation?
Rendering only the rows currently visible (plus a small buffer) and recycling them while scrolling, so very long lists keep a small DOM and stay fast.
What does useTransition do?
Marks a state update as non-urgent so React can keep the UI responsive to urgent updates (typing, clicks) while rendering the heavy update in the background; isPending shows progress.
What are Core Web Vitals?
LCP (loading speed of main content), INP (responsiveness to interactions) and CLS (visual stability): the user-centred metrics used to measure real-world performance.

topics.name: Testing Components with Vitest and React Testing Library

beginner.content:
Why and how we test

• Tests catch regressions and let you refactor safely. The pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration/component tests, a few end-to-end tests.
• Vitest (Vite-native, Jest-compatible API) runs the tests; React Testing Library (RTL) renders components and queries them like a user would. Test behaviour (what the user sees and does), not implementation details (state variables, internal methods).
• Setup: npm i -D vitest jsdom @testing-library/react @testing-library/user-event @testing-library/jest-dom.

intermediate.content:
Writing a component test

• Arrange (render), Act (user events), Assert (what is on screen).
• Query priority (best to worst): getByRole (with name), getByLabelText, getByPlaceholderText, getByText, then getByTestId as a last resort. This also verifies accessibility.
• getBy* throws if missing, queryBy* returns null (use to assert absence), findBy* waits (async).
• Use userEvent (realistic typing/clicking) instead of fireEvent.

expert.content:
Testing forms and callbacks

• Pass vi.fn() mocks as callback props and assert on calls: expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledWith({...}).
• For validation, assert that error messages appear (findByRole("alert")) and that the callback was not called.
• Prefer testing through the public UI: type into labelled inputs, click the submit button.
• Snapshot tests are brittle; use them sparingly for small, stable output.

interviewQA: What does React Testing Library encourage?
Testing from the user's point of view: render the component, find elements by role/label/text, interact with userEvent and assert on visible output rather than on internal state.
getBy vs queryBy vs findBy?
getBy* throws if nothing matches, queryBy* returns null (use for asserting absence), findBy* returns a promise that waits for the element (use for async UI).
Why prefer getByRole?
It mirrors how assistive technologies see the page, so tests double as accessibility checks and survive markup refactors.

topics.name: Mocking APIs with MSW, Testing Hooks, Router and Context

beginner.content:
Mock the network, not the component

• MSW (Mock Service Worker) intercepts HTTP requests at the network level and returns fake responses. Your component code (fetch/axios/TanStack Query) stays untouched, so the test exercises real integration.
• Define handlers per endpoint; override them in a single test to simulate errors (500, network failure) and empty data.
• Test all four states: loading, success, empty, error.

intermediate.content:
Wrapping with providers: Router, Query, Context

• Components that use useNavigate, useQuery or useContext need their providers in tests. Write a custom render helper that wraps the UI in MemoryRouter, a fresh QueryClient (retry off) and your context providers.
• Use MemoryRouter initialEntries={["/courses/5"]} to start at a route and assert on navigation by checking what renders.
• Create a new QueryClient per test to avoid cache leaking between tests.

expert.content:
Testing custom hooks and async behaviour

• renderHook runs a hook inside a test component. Call state-changing functions inside act() and read result.current.
• For timers (debounce) use fake timers: vi.useFakeTimers() and vi.advanceTimersByTime(300).
• Use waitFor for assertions that become true later; never use arbitrary setTimeout sleeps in tests.
• Keep tests independent, fast and deterministic: no real network, no shared mutable state.

interviewQA: Why use MSW instead of mocking fetch?
MSW intercepts requests at the network layer, so the app uses its real fetch/axios code paths. Handlers are reusable across tests, the browser and Storybook, and are easy to override for error cases.
How do you test a component that uses React Router or Context?
Wrap it with the needed providers in a custom render helper (MemoryRouter, QueryClientProvider, context providers), starting at a specific route if needed.
How do you test a custom hook?
Use renderHook, wrap state updates in act(), assert on result.current, and use fake timers or waitFor for time-based behaviour.

topics.name: End-to-End Tests, Coverage and Continuous Integration

beginner.content:
End-to-end tests with Playwright

• E2E tests drive a real browser through complete user journeys (sign up, add to cart, pay) against a running app and test API. They catch integration problems unit tests cannot, but are slower and more fragile: cover the critical paths only.
• Playwright auto-waits for elements, runs Chromium/Firefox/WebKit, records traces and screenshots on failure. Use role/label locators, not CSS selectors.

intermediate.content:
Coverage and what to test

• Coverage (vitest run --coverage) shows which lines run during tests. Use it to find untested code, not as a target: 100% coverage can still miss behaviour.
• Test: business rules and utilities (unit), components with logic and branching (component tests), critical flows (E2E), bugs you fixed (regression tests).
• Do not test: library internals, trivial markup, implementation details like private state.
• Accessibility checks in tests: jest-axe/vitest-axe catches many a11y bugs automatically.

expert.content:
Run tests automatically in CI

• Every push and pull request should run lint, type-check, unit tests and build; failing checks block the merge. Run E2E against a preview deployment or a started server.
• Cache node_modules, fail fast, upload Playwright reports as artifacts.
• Keep the suite fast (under a few minutes) or it will be ignored; quarantine flaky tests and fix them.
codeExamples:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npx tsc --noEmit
      - run: npm test -- --run --coverage
      - run: npm run build
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: npx playwright test
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: failure()
        with: { name: playwright-report, path: playwright-report/ }

interviewQA: Unit vs integration vs end-to-end tests?

Unit tests check small pieces in isolation (fast, many). Integration/component tests check several parts together (a component with its hooks and mocked API). End-to-end tests drive the whole app in a real browser (slow, few, critical flows).
Is 100% code coverage a good goal?
No. Coverage only shows lines executed, not whether behaviour is verified. Use it to find gaps and focus on meaningful assertions on important logic.
Why run tests in CI?
So every change is verified automatically in a clean environment, preventing regressions from reaching main and giving fast feedback to the whole team.

subTopics.name: Phase 14 · Security and Accessibility (Essential for production)

topics.name: Security: XSS, CSRF and Safe React Code

beginner.content:
XSS (cross-site scripting)

• XSS lets an attacker run their script in your page (steal data, act as the user). It happens when untrusted text becomes HTML or script.
• React helps: values in { } are escaped. The dangerous escapes are dangerouslySetInnerHTML, href="javascript:..." from user data, eval/new Function, and injecting HTML through refs/innerHTML.
• If you must render HTML (a rich-text comment), sanitise it with DOMPurify first.

intermediate.content:
CSRF and cookies

• CSRF: another site makes the user's browser send an authenticated request to your API (the browser attaches cookies automatically). It only matters when you authenticate with cookies.
• Defences: SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies, CSRF tokens (Spring Security supports them), verifying Origin/Referer, and requiring a custom header or JSON content type.
• Cookie flags: HttpOnly (JS cannot read it, defeating token theft by XSS), Secure (HTTPS only), SameSite.
• Use POST/PUT/DELETE for state-changing requests, never GET.

expert.content:
Secure coding checklist for React apps

• Never trust the client: hiding a button or route does not protect data. The server must authenticate and authorise every request.
• Secrets: anything in the bundle or VITE_* variables is public. Keep API secrets on the server.
• Dependencies: npm audit, lock files, Dependabot/Renovate, avoid abandoned packages. Supply-chain attacks target node_modules.
• CSP header (script-src 'self') limits XSS impact; HTTPS + HSTS; X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff; frame-ancestors against clickjacking.
• Redirects/URLs: validate redirect parameters to avoid open redirects; do not render user-supplied URLs unchecked.
• Do not log sensitive data; mask tokens and personal data in error reports.

interviewQA: How does React protect against XSS and where can it still happen?

React escapes values embedded in JSX. XSS can still occur via dangerouslySetInnerHTML, javascript: URLs, eval, direct innerHTML on refs, or vulnerable third-party code. Sanitise HTML with DOMPurify and validate URLs.
What is CSRF and when does it apply?

An attacker's site triggers an authenticated request from the victim's browser. It applies when authentication relies on cookies sent automatically. Use SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens and Origin checks.
Why is hiding a route or button in React not security?
Client code can be modified or bypassed (devtools, curl). Authorisation must be enforced by the API on every request; the UI only improves experience.

topics.name: Authentication, Authorization, JWT, Secure Sessions and CORS

beginner.content:
Authentication vs authorization

• Authentication = who are you (login). Authorization = what may you do (roles, permissions, ownership).
• Role-based access control (RBAC): the server returns the user's roles/permissions; React uses them to show or hide UI, while the API enforces them (@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") in Spring Security).
• Apply the principle of least privilege and check ownership server-side (a user may edit only their own records).

intermediate.content:
JWT and secure session management

• A JWT is a signed token (header.payload.signature) carrying claims (user id, roles, expiry). It is signed, not encrypted: never put secrets in it.
• Use short-lived access tokens (5-15 min) plus a refresh token (days) stored in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie and rotated on use; revoke on logout/compromise.
• Alternative: classic server-side sessions with an HttpOnly cookie. Simpler to revoke; great for a single Spring Boot back end.
• Keep the access token in memory (a variable), not localStorage; rebuild it from the refresh cookie on page load.
• Always verify the signature, issuer, audience and expiry on the server.

expert.content:
CORS in depth

• The browser blocks a page from reading responses of another origin (scheme + host + port) unless the server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin. It is enforced by the browser, configured on the server.
• Non-simple requests (JSON body, Authorization header, PUT/DELETE) trigger a preflight OPTIONS request that must succeed.
• With cookies you need credentials: "include" and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true with an explicit origin (never *).
• Best practice: avoid CORS completely by serving the SPA and API from the same origin (reverse proxy), or proxy in dev. Allow only known origins, methods and headers.

interviewQA: Authentication vs authorization?
Authentication verifies identity (login). Authorization decides what an authenticated user may do (roles, permissions, ownership) and must be enforced on the server.
Is a JWT encrypted?
No. A standard JWT is signed (integrity) but its payload is only base64url-encoded, so anyone can read it. Never put secrets in it, and always verify the signature and expiry on the server.
How can you avoid CORS entirely?
Serve the front end and API from the same origin behind a reverse proxy (nginx), or use the dev server proxy in development. Otherwise configure CORS on the server with explicit origins.

topics.name: Accessibility (a11y) in React

beginner.content:
Build for everyone

• Accessibility means people using keyboards, screen readers, zoom or voice control can use your app. It is also a legal requirement in many places and improves SEO and usability for everyone.
• Use semantic HTML first: <button> for actions, <a> for navigation, <nav>, <main>, <h1>-<h6> in order, <label> for inputs, <table> for data. A <div onClick> is not focusable and has no role.
• Provide text alternatives: alt on images (empty alt="" for decorative), accessible names for icon buttons (aria-label).

intermediate.content:
Keyboard, focus and ARIA

• Everything must work with the keyboard: Tab order follows the DOM, focus is visible (do not remove outlines), Escape closes dialogs, arrow keys move within composite widgets.
• Manage focus on route changes and dialogs: move focus to the new page heading or the dialog, trap it inside a modal, and restore it on close.
• ARIA adds meaning when HTML cannot: aria-expanded, aria-controls, aria-live (announce updates), role="alert". First rule of ARIA: do not use it if a native element does the job; wrong ARIA is worse than none.
• Provide a skip link ("Skip to content") for keyboard users.

expert.content:
Forms, colour, motion and testing

• Every input has a visible <label>; errors are tied to the field with aria-describedby and announced with role="alert"; required fields are marked in text, not colour alone.
• Contrast: at least 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text and UI components (WCAG AA). Never use colour as the only signal.
• Respect prefers-reduced-motion and avoid auto-playing content; support zoom to 200% without horizontal scrolling.
• Test: eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y, vitest-axe/axe DevTools, Lighthouse, keyboard-only walkthrough and a screen reader (NVDA, VoiceOver).

interviewQA: Why use a button instead of a clickable div?
A button is focusable, activates with Enter/Space and exposes the correct role to assistive technology. A div needs tabIndex, key handlers and ARIA to imitate it, and still usually falls short.
How do you manage focus in a modal?
Move focus into the dialog on open, trap Tab inside it, close on Escape, set role="dialog" aria-modal and a label, and return focus to the element that opened it on close.
What is aria-live for?
It makes screen readers announce dynamic content changes (search result counts, status messages) without moving focus. Use polite for non-urgent and role="alert" for urgent messages.

topics.name: Error Handling and Error Boundaries

beginner.content:
Where errors can happen in React

• Render errors (exceptions while rendering) unmount the whole tree and show a blank page unless caught by an error boundary.
• Event handler and async errors are not caught by boundaries: use try/catch (and .catch on promises) and show an error state.
• An error boundary is a class component with static getDerivedStateFromError (switch to fallback UI) and componentDidCatch (log). The react-error-boundary package provides a ready-made component and hooks.

intermediate.content:
react-error-boundary and placement strategy

• Place boundaries at several levels: app-wide (last resort), per route (a broken page keeps the navigation), and around risky widgets (charts, third-party embeds) so one failure does not take down the page.
• resetKeys resets the boundary when something changes (for example the route). The fallback receives error and resetErrorBoundary.
• Show a helpful message, offer retry, and never expose stack traces to users.

expert.content:
A complete error-handling strategy

• Validate inputs and API data early (Zod) so bad data fails with a clear message.
• Normalise errors from the API into one shape and map HTTP status to user-friendly text (401 login, 403 no access, 404 not found, 429 slow down, 5xx try later).
• Global handlers: window.addEventListener("error") and "unhandledrejection" report to your monitoring service. TanStack Query: onError or a global QueryCache handler.
