• User feedback: toast for transient failures, inline errors for forms, full-page fallback for fatal errors. Log technical details with a request id; do not show them to users.

interviewQA: What do error boundaries catch and not catch?

They catch errors during rendering, in lifecycle methods and constructors of the tree below them. They do not catch errors in event handlers, asynchronous code, server-side rendering or in the boundary itself.
Why are error boundaries class components?
Only class components can implement getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch. There is no hook equivalent, so use a small class or the react-error-boundary library.
Where should you place error boundaries?
At the app level (last resort), around each route/page, and around independent risky widgets, so failures stay contained and the rest of the UI keeps working.

topics.name: Higher-Order Components, Portals and Strict Mode

beginner.content:
Higher-Order Components (HOC)

• A HOC is a function that takes a component and returns a new component with extra behaviour: withAuth(Dashboard), withLoading(List). Libraries such as Redux's old connect and React Router's old withRouter used them.
• Conventions: do not mutate the original component, pass through unrelated props, set a displayName, hoist statics, and never create a HOC inside render (new component type each render resets state).
• Today hooks and composition replace most HOCs, but you will meet them in older codebases and for cross-cutting wrappers (auth guards, error boundaries, analytics).

intermediate.content:
Portals

• createPortal(children, domNode) renders children into a different DOM node (usually document.body) while keeping them in the React tree. Events still bubble through the React hierarchy and context still works.
• Use it for modals, tooltips, dropdowns, toasts that must escape overflow: hidden, z-index stacking contexts or transforms of a parent.
• Remember accessibility: focus management, role="dialog", Escape to close, and scroll locking.

expert.content:
React Strict Mode

• <StrictMode> is a development-only tool that finds bugs early: it renders components twice to expose impure render code, runs effects setup + cleanup + setup on mount to check cleanup logic, warns about deprecated APIs and detects unsafe patterns. It has no effect in production builds.
• If a component behaves wrongly in Strict Mode (double fetch, double subscription, duplicated analytics event) it has a real bug: missing cleanup or an impure render, not "a Strict Mode bug".
• Fix: return cleanup from effects (abort, unsubscribe, clearInterval), keep render pure, and make effects idempotent. Do not remove StrictMode to hide the problem.

interviewQA: What is a higher-order component?
A function that takes a component and returns an enhanced component (withAuth, withLoading). It reuses behaviour across components; hooks and composition now cover most cases.
Why use portals?
To render UI like modals, tooltips and dropdowns outside their parent DOM node (escaping overflow/z-index clipping) while keeping them in the React tree for props, context and event bubbling.
Why does my effect run twice in development?
StrictMode intentionally mounts, cleans up and remounts components to verify that effects clean up properly. It does not happen in production; add proper cleanup instead of removing StrictMode.

topics.name: Concurrent Rendering, Suspense for Data and Server-Side Rendering

beginner.content:
Concurrent rendering

• In React 18+, rendering can be interrupted, paused and resumed. React can start rendering an update, pause to handle an urgent event (typing), then continue. This keeps the UI responsive without you writing any scheduling code.
• You opt in through APIs: createRoot, useTransition/startTransition (mark non-urgent updates), useDeferredValue, and Suspense.
• Consequences: render functions must be pure and may run more than once; never rely on render running exactly once or on side effects in render.

intermediate.content:
Suspense for data and streaming

• Suspense lets a component "wait" for something (code, data) and show a fallback meanwhile. Data libraries (TanStack Query useSuspenseQuery, Relay) and the React 19 use(promise) hook integrate with it.
• Benefits: no manual isLoading flags, declarative loading boundaries, no waterfalls when you fetch in parallel above the boundary.
• Wrap in an error boundary to handle failures and keep promises stable (created outside render or cached), otherwise you create a new request every render.

expert.content:
SSR, hydration and Server Components

• Client-side rendering (CSR): the browser downloads JS, then renders (blank page first, weaker SEO). Server-side rendering (SSR): the server sends ready HTML, then JS hydrates it (attaches event handlers). Static generation (SSG) pre-renders at build time.
• Hydration requires the server and client output to match; things like Date.now(), Math.random(), or window in render cause hydration mismatches.
• React Server Components (Next.js App Router, React Router framework mode) run only on the server and send no JS for themselves: they can read databases directly. Interactive pieces are marked "use client".
• Choose a framework (Next.js, Remix/React Router) when you need SEO, fast first paint or server data access; a Vite SPA is fine for authenticated dashboards like an LMS back office.

interviewQA: What is concurrent rendering?

React can interrupt, pause and resume rendering so urgent updates (typing, clicking) are handled immediately while non-urgent ones render in the background, using APIs like useTransition, useDeferredValue and Suspense.
What is hydration?
The step where React attaches event handlers and state to HTML that was rendered on the server. The initial client render must match the server HTML or React reports a hydration mismatch.
When would you choose Next.js or SSR over a Vite SPA?
When you need SEO for public pages, fast first contentful paint, or server-side data access. For authenticated dashboards behind a login, a Vite SPA is often simpler.

topics.name: Environment Variables and Production Builds

beginner.content:
Configuration without code changes

• Different environments (development, test, staging, production) need different settings: API URL, feature flags, analytics keys. Keep them out of the source code.
• Vite loads .env, .env.development, .env.production (and .local variants). Only variables starting with VITE_ are exposed to the browser as import.meta.env.VITE_*. import.meta.env.MODE, DEV, PROD are built in.
• Variables are inlined at build time. Changing one requires a rebuild; "build once, deploy anywhere" needs a runtime config (/config.json fetched at start).

intermediate.content:
Secrets and runtime config

• Never put secrets in VITE_* (database passwords, private API keys, JWT signing keys): they are plain text in the bundle. Public identifiers (Sentry DSN, Google client id, map key restricted by domain) are fine.
• Keep real secrets on the server (Spring Boot application-prod.properties via environment variables, a secrets manager) and call them through your API.
• Commit .env.example, not .env.local; add .env*.local to .gitignore.
• For one image deployed to many environments, load config at runtime.

expert.content:
Production build checklist

• npm run build creates optimised, minified, hashed files in dist/; preview locally with npm run preview. Test the production build, not only the dev server.
• Check: no console.log noise, source maps uploaded to the error tracker but not served publicly, correct base if hosted under a sub-path, favicon/meta tags, 404 fallback to index.html for client-side routing.
• Run lint, type-check, tests and a Lighthouse audit before release. Version the build and expose it (VITE_APP_VERSION) so bug reports include it.

interviewQA: Why must secrets not be in VITE_ variables?
Vite inlines them into the client bundle at build time, so anyone can read them in the browser. Keep secrets on the server and expose only public configuration.
When are Vite env variables resolved?
At build time. Changing a value requires a rebuild. For runtime configuration load a config file (config.json) when the app starts.
What should you check before shipping a production build?
Run lint, type-check, tests and the build; preview it locally; verify routes fall back to index.html, source maps are not public, env values are correct and Lighthouse/Core Web Vitals are acceptable.

topics.name: Deploying React: Ubuntu, Nginx, Spring Boot and Docker

beginner.content:
What deployment means for an SPA

• npm run build produces static files (HTML, JS, CSS, images). Any web server can host them. The server must (1) serve index.html for unknown paths (client-side routing), (2) proxy /api to the back end, (3) serve over HTTPS, (4) set caching and security headers.
• Common setups: Nginx on an Ubuntu VM in front of a Spring Boot jar; the Spring Boot jar serving the built files itself; a static host/CDN (S3 + CloudFront, Netlify, Vercel) plus an API elsewhere.

intermediate.content:
HTTPS and the Spring Boot service

• HTTPS is mandatory (service workers, secure cookies, trust). Get free certificates with Let's Encrypt: sudo apt install certbot python3-certbot-nginx then sudo certbot --nginx -d app.javaschoollab.com; it edits Nginx and renews automatically.
• Run the back end as a systemd service so it starts on boot and restarts on failure; pass secrets as environment variables or an env file with restricted permissions.
• Open only ports 80/443 (and SSH) in the firewall: sudo ufw allow 'Nginx Full'; keep Spring Boot bound to localhost.
codeExamples:
# /etc/systemd/system/javaschoollab.service
[Unit]
Description=JavaSchoolLab API
After=network.target mysql.service

[Service]
User=jsl
EnvironmentFile=/etc/javaschoollab/env          # SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD=..., JWT_SECRET=... (chmod 600)
ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -jar /opt/javaschoollab/app.jar --server.address=127.0.0.1 --server.port=8080
Restart=on-failure
SuccessExitStatus=143

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

# sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl enable --now javaschoollab
# sudo ufw allow OpenSSH && sudo ufw allow 'Nginx Full' && sudo ufw enable
# sudo certbot --nginx -d app.javaschoollab.com   (adds HTTPS and auto-renewal)
# journalctl -u javaschoollab -f                   (follow the application logs)

expert.content:
Docker, zero-downtime releases and alternatives

• A multi-stage Dockerfile builds the app in a Node image and serves dist from a tiny Nginx image: reproducible, identical everywhere. Compose it with the API and database.
• Releases: build, upload to a new directory, switch a symlink (current) and reload Nginx; keep the previous release for instant rollback. Hashed asset names let old and new versions coexist.
• Single jar: copy dist/ into Spring Boot static/ (or the Maven frontend plugin) so one process serves the site and API on one origin, avoiding CORS. Add a controller that forwards unknown routes to index.html.
• Static hosting + CDN gives global speed with no server to maintain; configure the SPA fallback rule (/* /index.html 200).
codeExamples:
# Dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
ARG VITE_API_URL=/api
ENV VITE_API_URL=$VITE_API_URL
RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
EXPOSE 80
HEALTHCHECK CMD wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1/ >/dev/null || exit 1

# docker-compose.yml
# services:
#   web: { build: ./frontend, ports: ["80:80"], depends_on: [api] }
#   api: { image: javaschoollab/api:1.0, environment: { SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod }, expose: ["8080"] }
#   db:  { image: mysql:8, environment: { MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db }, volumes: [dbdata:/var/lib/mysql] }

# Atomic release with rollback
# rsync -a dist/ /var/www/releases/2026-10-20/ && ln -sfn /var/www/releases/2026-10-20 /var/www/current && sudo nginx -s reload
# rollback: ln -sfn /var/www/releases/<previous> /var/www/current && sudo nginx -s reload

interviewQA: Why does the server need a try_files /index.html rule?
With client-side routing, URLs like /courses/5 are not files. The server must return index.html for unknown paths so the React router can render the route, instead of a 404 on refresh.
Why put Nginx in front of Spring Boot?

It terminates HTTPS, serves static files and caches efficiently, compresses, applies security headers, and proxies /api to the app, keeping Spring Boot private on localhost and avoiding CORS with one origin.
How do you roll back a bad release?
Keep each release in its own directory (or image tag) and switch a symlink/tag back to the previous one, then reload Nginx. Hashed asset names let old and new files coexist.

topics.name: Git Workflow and CI/CD Pipelines

beginner.content:
Git essentials for teams

• Git tracks changes as commits on branches. Core commands: git clone, status, add, commit, push, pull, branch, switch, merge, rebase, log, diff, stash.
• Workflow: create a short-lived feature branch from main, commit small logical changes, push, open a pull request, get review and green checks, then merge (squash or rebase) and delete the branch.
• Write meaningful commit messages (imperative: "Add course search"), commit often, never commit secrets or node_modules.
codeExamples:
git switch main && git pull
git switch -c feature/course-search

# ...edit files...
git add src/features/search/
git commit -m "Add debounced course search with TanStack Query"
git push -u origin feature/course-search          # then open a pull request on GitHub

# keep the branch up to date
git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main

# undo safely
git restore src/App.jsx                           # discard local edits to one file
git revert <commit>                               # new commit that undoes an old one (safe on shared branches)
git stash push -m "wip" && git stash pop

# .gitignore
# node_modules/
# dist/
# .env.local

intermediate.content:
Branching strategies and conventions

• Trunk-based development (short branches, merge to main daily, feature flags) suits continuous delivery. Git Flow (develop, release, hotfix branches) fits scheduled releases.
• Protect main: require pull requests, reviews and passing checks; forbid force-push.
• Conventional Commits (feat:, fix:, docs:, chore:) enable automatic changelogs and semantic versioning.
• Semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; tag releases (git tag v1.4.0).
• Resolve merge conflicts calmly: read both sides, keep the intended result, run the tests, then continue the merge/rebase.
codeExamples:
# Conventional commits
git commit -m "feat(courses): add React roadmap phases"
git commit -m "fix(router): redirect to login on expired session"

# release
git tag -a v1.4.0 -m "React roadmap and TypeScript lessons"
git push origin v1.4.0

# conflict markers
# <<<<<<< HEAD
# your change
# =======
# their change
# >>>>>>> feature/x
# edit to the final text, remove the markers, then:
git add path/to/file && git rebase --continue

expert.content:
CI/CD with GitHub Actions

• CI (continuous integration): on every push/PR run install, lint, type-check, tests and build. CD (continuous delivery/deployment): on merge to main build an artifact (image or dist), deploy to staging automatically and to production automatically or after approval.
• Store secrets (SSH key, registry token) in GitHub Secrets, never in the repo. Use environments with required reviewers for production.
• Keep pipelines fast: cache dependencies, run jobs in parallel, fail early. Make deployments idempotent and reversible.
codeExamples:
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: Build and deploy
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint && npx tsc --noEmit && npm test -- --run
      - run: npm run build
        env: { VITE_API_URL: https://api.javaschoollab.com }
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: dist, path: dist }

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production                      # can require a manual approval
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with: { name: dist, path: dist }
      - name: Upload to server
        run: |
          echo "${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KEY }}" > key && chmod 600 key
          rsync -az --delete -e "ssh -i key -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new" dist/ deploy@app.javaschoollab.com:/var/www/javaschoollab/
      - name: Smoke test
        run: curl -fsS https://app.javaschoollab.com/ | grep -q '<div id="root">'

interviewQA: Merge vs rebase?
Merge joins histories with a merge commit and preserves the real history. Rebase replays your commits on top of the target branch for a linear history; do not rebase commits that others already use.
What is the difference between CI and CD?
CI automatically builds and tests every change. CD automatically delivers (or deploys) successful builds to staging/production, often with a manual approval gate for production.
Where do deployment secrets belong?
In the CI system's secret store (GitHub Secrets/environments) or a secrets manager, never in the repository or the front-end bundle.

topics.name: Monitoring: Errors, Performance and Logs

beginner.content:
You cannot fix what you cannot see

• Users rarely report errors. Monitoring collects them automatically: JavaScript exceptions, failed API calls, slow pages and unusual behaviour, with context (URL, browser, user id, release version).
• Typical stack: Sentry (errors and performance), web-vitals + analytics (real-user performance), uptime checks (UptimeRobot, Pingdom), server logs and metrics (Spring Boot Actuator, Prometheus/Grafana, ELK).
• Upload source maps to the tracker so minified stack traces become readable, but do not serve them publicly.

intermediate.content:
Real-user performance and product analytics

• Lab tools (Lighthouse) show potential; real-user monitoring (RUM) shows what users experience on real devices and networks. Send web-vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) to your backend or analytics.
• Track key flows (sign-up funnel, course completion) with privacy-respecting analytics (Plausible, PostHog, GA4 with consent). Respect GDPR/DPDP: obtain consent, anonymise IPs, avoid personal data in events.
• Set budgets and alerts: error rate spike, LCP regression, 5xx rate, uptime.

expert.content:
Logging, alerts and incident response

• Structured logs (JSON with level, timestamp, request id, user id) are searchable. Add a correlation id header on every request (X-Request-Id) and log it on both sides to trace a failure across front end and API.
• Alert on symptoms users feel (errors, latency, downtime), route alerts to a channel with an owner, and keep a short runbook.
• After an incident, write a post-mortem (timeline, root cause, fix, prevention). Add a regression test.
• Do not log secrets, tokens or personal data; rotate logs and set retention limits.

interviewQA: Why use an error tracking service like Sentry?
Users rarely report bugs. It captures exceptions automatically with stack traces (via source maps), release, browser and user context, groups duplicates and alerts you, so you can fix issues quickly.
What is real-user monitoring?
Collecting performance metrics (Core Web Vitals) from actual users' browsers, which reflects real devices and networks, unlike lab tests such as Lighthouse run on one machine.
What is a correlation id?
A unique id sent with a request and included in logs on every system it touches, so a failure seen in the browser can be traced to the exact server log lines.

Component - Reusable, self-contained piece of UI
Functional component - Component written as a plain JS function
Class component - Component written as an ES6 class extending React.Component
Props - Read-only data passed from parent to child component
State - Mutable data local to a component, triggers re-render on change
Props vs State - Props are external/immutable, state is internal/mutable
useState - Hook to add state to a functional component
useEffect - Hook to run side effects after render (data fetching, subscriptions)
useEffect cleanup - Return a function from useEffect to clean up on unmount
Dependency array - Controls when useEffect re-runs
useRef - Hook to persist a mutable value/DOM reference without re-rendering
useContext - Hook to consume a Context value without prop drilling
useMemo - Hook to memoize expensive computed values
useCallback - Hook to memoize function references between renders
Custom hooks - Reusable functions starting with 'use' that encapsulate hook logic
Component lifecycle - Mounting, updating, unmounting phases
componentDidMount/Update/WillUnmount - Class component lifecycle methods
Conditional rendering - Rendering JSX based on conditions (ternary, &&, if)
Lists & keys - key prop helps React identify changed/added/removed list items
Event handling - Attaching handlers like onClick, onChange in JSX using camelCase
Controlled component - Form input value driven by React state
Uncontrolled component - Form input value managed by the DOM itself (via ref)
Lifting state up - Moving shared state to the closest common ancestor
Context API - Share data across component tree without passing props manually
Virtual DOM - In-memory representation of the real DOM for efficient updates
Reconciliation - React's diffing algorithm to update only changed DOM nodes
React.memo - Higher-order component that memoizes a component to avoid re-renders
React Router - Library for client-side routing/navigation in React apps
<Routes>/<Route> - Define URL paths and matching components
useNavigate - Hook to programmatically navigate between routes
useParams - Hook to read dynamic route parameters
Fragments (<>...</>) - Group elements without adding extra DOM nodes
Prop drilling - Passing props through many nested levels of components
SPA - Single Page Application, updates content without full page reload
React supports server-side rendering (SSR) and static site generation (SSG)
